skills.name: Laws of exponents
skills.intro_md: When you multiply powers with the same base you add the exponents; when you divide them you subtract; when a power is raised to a power you multiply.
misconceptions: Multiplying the exponents when multiplying powers
Applying the exponent to the coefficient only

skills.name: Scientific notation
skills.intro_md: Scientific notation writes a number as a value between 1 and 10 times a power of ten. A positive exponent means a big number, a negative exponent means a small one.
misconceptions: Keeping the decimal in the wrong place (the first factor must be 1 to 10)
Sign error when moving the decimal to the right

skills.name: Simplifying linear expressions
skills.intro_md: Combine like terms by adding their coefficients, and use the distributive property to remove brackets before combining.
misconceptions: Distributing to the first term only
Dropping the sign in front of a subtracted bracket

skills.name: Equations with variables on both sides
skills.intro_md: Move every variable term to one side and every constant to the other, then divide by the coefficient. Whatever you do to one side you must do to the other.
misconceptions: Moving a term without changing its sign
Dividing only one side by the coefficient

skills.name: Solving systems by substitution
skills.intro_md: When one equation already gives you y (or x) in terms of the other variable, replace that variable in the second equation. You get one equation with one unknown.
misconceptions: Substituting into the same equation instead of the other one
Stopping after finding one variable and forgetting the other

skills.name: The Pythagorean theorem
skills.intro_md: In a right triangle the two legs satisfy a² + b² = c², where c is always the side across from the right angle (the longest side).
misconceptions: Putting a leg where the hypotenuse belongs
Adding the squares instead of subtracting to find a missing leg

skills.name: Solving one-variable equations
skills.intro_md: Undo operations in reverse order: first the addition or subtraction, then the multiplication or division, working towards x on its own.
misconceptions: Dividing before undoing the constant
Losing the negative sign when dividing

skills.name: Linear equations with variables on both sides
skills.intro_md: Collect the variable terms on one side and the numbers on the other. If brackets are involved, distribute first.
misconceptions: Distributing to only one term in the bracket
Sign errors when a bracket is subtracted

skills.name: Linear inequalities
skills.intro_md: Solve inequalities like equations, with one exception: multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number flips the inequality sign.
misconceptions: Forgetting to flip the sign when dividing by a negative
Treating 'at most' as a strict inequality

skills.name: Slope and intercepts
skills.intro_md: Slope is rise over run: (y₂ − y₁) / (x₂ − x₁). In y = mx + b, m is the slope and b is the y-intercept.
misconceptions: Putting the change in x on top
Reading the intercept as a point instead of the y-value

skills.name: Systems of equations by substitution
skills.intro_md: Solve one equation for a variable, substitute it into the other, solve, then back-substitute to find the second variable.
misconceptions: Substituting back into the rearranged equation
Reporting only one of the two values

skills.name: Factoring quadratics
skills.intro_md: For x² + bx + c, find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b. Those become the two constants in the factored form.
misconceptions: Choosing numbers that multiply to b instead of c
Losing a sign when c is negative

skills.name: One-dimensional kinematics
skills.intro_md: The four constant-acceleration equations connect v, v₀, a, t and Δx. Pick the one that contains what you know and what you need.
misconceptions: Using a constant-acceleration equation when the acceleration changes
Sign errors from mixing up v and v₀

skills.name: Newton's second law
skills.intro_md: ΣF = ma uses the net force, not one force. Draw the free-body diagram first, then add the components along the direction of motion.
misconceptions: Using the applied force instead of the net force
Forgetting that the normal force is not always mg

skills.name: Work done by a constant force
skills.intro_md: W = F d cos θ uses the component of the force along the displacement. A force perpendicular to the motion does no work.
misconceptions: Ignoring the angle and using F·d
Counting friction as positive work

skills.name: Work done by a varying force
skills.intro_md: When the force changes, work is the area under the force-versus-position graph, not force times distance.
misconceptions: Using the final force for the whole distance
Treating a triangular area as a rectangle

skills.name: The work-energy theorem
skills.intro_md: The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy: W_net = ΔK. It is often easier than tracking forces through time.
misconceptions: Using only one force's work for W_net
Forgetting that friction does negative work

skills.name: Momentum and impulse in one dimension
skills.intro_md: p = mv, and impulse J = FΔt equals the change in momentum. In a collision with no external force, total momentum is conserved.
misconceptions: Forgetting that momentum is a vector
Using kinetic energy conservation for every collision

skills.name: Linear equations and systems
skills.intro_md: SAT linear questions reward translating words into equations and solving systems efficiently rather than elegantly.
misconceptions: Solving for x when the question asks for an expression
One solution when the system has two unknowns

skills.name: Percent change and percent of
skills.intro_md: Percent change is (new − old) / old × 100. A percent decrease multiplies by (1 − rate); a percent increase multiplies by (1 + rate).
misconceptions: Dividing by the new value instead of the original
Adding successive percentages instead of multiplying the factors

skills.name: Ratios, rates and proportions
skills.intro_md: Set up a proportion with matching units, then cross-multiply. For part-to-whole ratios, the total is the sum of the parts.
misconceptions: Mixing units in the two sides of a proportion
Treating a part-to-part ratio as part-to-whole

skills.name: Area and perimeter
skills.intro_md: Know the rectangle, triangle and circle formulas cold, and split composite shapes into pieces you can measure.
misconceptions: Using the diameter instead of the radius
Forgetting to halve for a triangle's area

skills.name: Function notation and composition
skills.intro_md: f(3) means substitute 3 for x. f(g(2)) means evaluate g(2) first, then put that result into f.
misconceptions: Multiplying f by the input instead of substituting
Evaluating the outer function first in a composition

questions.stem: Simplify: 2³ · 2⁴

You added the bases as well. Only the exponents change.

hints: The exponent outside the bracket applies to every factor inside.

You moved the decimal one place too far.

You added the coefficients (2 + 3). Multiply them.

You added the speeds instead of multiplying.
You divided. Distance is speed × time.

Adding x terms does not change the power of x.
You subtracted the coefficients.

You did not combine the −5x with the 6x.

You distributed the −2 to x only, not to −3.

You divided 22 by 5 before undoing the +7.

You subtracted 4 instead of adding it.

options.why: Check: 2(5) = 10 and 4(2) − 10 = −2. They do not match.

questions.stem: A 60 kg rider stands on a scale in an elevator and the scale reads 720 N. What is the elevator's acceleration? (g = 9.8 m/s²)

You used half the friction force.

hints: f = μN = μmg on a flat floor.

questions.stem: The net work done on a 2 kg block starting from rest is 25 J. What is its final speed?

options.why: You took the square root of 25/2.
That is K/m, not √(2K/m).
You used the work as a speed.

questions.stem: A force F = 4x (newtons, with x in metres) acts from x = 0 to x = 3 m. How much work is done?

You used ½kx without squaring x.

You used half the distance.

You used ½k(0.4)² with k doubled.
